assignments.name: Attendance & participation — 24 of 30 classes for full credit (6 absences excused)

sections.Assignment Description:
1) 15% Attendance and Participation – attend 24 classes (of the 30 available) for full credit.
• You can miss a total of 6 classes without any penalty. You can miss class for any reason, which includes illness, emergencies,
just not wanting to come to class that day, or even if friends are coming to LA and you want to do some surfing. ALL
ABSENSES -up to 6- are excused and are treated the same; and you do not have to turn in any paperwork or let me know
you won’t be in class. But, if you miss more than 6 classes for any reason, each additional absence will be a deduction of
(approximately) 5 points from your attendance and participation grade, which equals (approximately) ½ of a point off your
final course grade. If you want to make up some points from missing more than 6 classes, you can do the extra credit
assignment…see the EXTRA CREDIT SECTION below.
• If you have a situation come up that will require that you miss more than 9 classes -which would equal missing 3 weeks of classes, I urge you to get ahold
of your advisor about dropping the course or taking an incomplete and finishing up during an upcoming semester; you simply cannot do well in the course
if you cannot come to class for whatever reason that may be.
IMPORTANT! Please read…
For lecture sessions (Tu/Th 2pm-3:20pm) you will use QWICKLY (via Brightspace) to log in within the first 3 minutes of class. Please make
sure to have a device with you in class that will allow you to sign in.
For lab/discussion sections, I will call role at the beginning of class. Arriving on time for classes is important to the flow of the class and it is
required. Clearly, sometime things happen and you might arrive late, but chronic lateness is unacceptable. To this end, every 3 late arrivals
will result in a 2-point deduction to your overall participation grade. No exceptions.
• LAB SECTIONS (Tuesdays):
• You must have completed all the assignments in the WEEKLY INSTRUCTION MODULE prior to attending your lab section, but you do not
need to turn in anything in prior to class, unless otherwise noted…just show up and be able to do the exercises and have the discussions
outlined in the WEEKLY MODULE INSTRUCTIONS.
• During lab sections, we will:
§ Have a short lecture on the week’s themes and assigned materials and watch some short films.
§ Do an experiential exercise and/or have a discussion about the current week’s materials and themes.
5

-- 5 of 16 --

• LECTURE SESSIONS (Tuesdays & Thursdays):
• During lecture sessions, we will:
• Have short lectures on the week’s themes and assigned materials, and watch some short films.
• Have ‘open’ time (most weeks) where you can work on your case study or the upcoming weeks’ assignments…such as viewing films,
reading, answering content study questions from the weekly module instructions, preparing for lab section exercises & discussions either
on your own or with other students, taking the weekly quiz (which you can do with other students!)…and get help from the instructor
with course content or your analytical case study (final paper).
• While lab sections are highly structured, lecture sessions are generally less so - other than the short lectures, which 1) allows for students
to get real-time, individualized help from the instructor, 2) provides a space for students to work on their own to complete weekly assignments,
3) presents opportunities for students to work on the course materials and their research projects with each other…students can even
complete the weekly quizzes together!

AI USE
Within this class, you are welcome to use AI. However, you should note that all large language models have a tendency to make up incorrect facts
and fake citations, data modeling tends to produce inaccurate outputs, and image generation is usually almost completely (and many times
offensively) wrong. In this course, you are fully responsible for the accuracy of all content you submit, including factual claims, interpretations,
and representations of evidence, regardless of whether the material was written by you or generated with the assistance of an AI tool or other
external source. Fabrication, falsification, or distortion of evidence violates USC’s definitions of academic dishonesty, whether produced manually
or via AI tools.
AI tools are an expected and legitimate part of the research and writing process in this course. However, they must be used as partners in thinking
and drafting, not as producers of your work. AI can help summarize, organize, or clarify information, but it cannot replace your analytical labor,
interpretive judgment, or engagement with course materials.
For exam essays and case study assignments (including the final paper), I am not looking for summaries. I am looking for evidence of nuanced
understanding, demonstrated through your ability to work across multiple types of data, evaluate their relationships, and explain how and why those
data matter. Strong work shows synthesis, comparison, and interpretation…not surface-level restatement.
Because generative AI can readily produce large amounts of information, simply providing more content does not demonstrate learning. High-quality
work synthesizes relevant evidence rather than compiling it. You should focus on integrating course concepts, examples, and terminology into
coherent analyses that demonstrate an understanding of how the material fits together, rather than presenting disconnected facts or exhaustive
summaries.
This level of analysis can only come from sustained engagement with the course: completing the readings, watching and reflecting on course
materials, participating in discussion, and thoughtfully working through the study questions. In short, meaningful scholarship requires real human
intellectual labor, not automated output. AI may support that process, but it cannot replace it. This means you should engage with AI tools to
brainstorm, do spelling and grammar checks, refine, clarify, or explore ideas, but the final product must clearly reflect your own holistic and nuanced
thinking, voice, and judgment.
Your work should demonstrate clear, original analysis; strong research; coherent writing; minimal grammar issues; authentic understanding of your
topic; and avoid AI-style vagueness, repetition, superficiality, and fabricated details. I will be looking for holistic & research informed thinking, well-
structured organization, detailed and varied evidence and data sources, personal voice, and human judgment throughout; and considering the help
AI can provide, your work must be extremely well written, free of spelling and grammatical errors, and follow all formatting and prompt instructions.
AI-generated content often lacks specificity, substitutes clichés for insight, and fabricates sources or examples. In contrast, human writing
demonstrates nuance, context awareness, meaningful synthesis, and intentional structure. These are not only academic expectations, but they are
also professional and transferable skills you will need in any discipline or industry moving forward. In addition, your work should clearly show active
participation and engagement with the specific themes, methodologies, and theoretical foundations we have explored in this course. Your writing
should reflect that you have taken this particular course; AI cannot replicate that level of engagement or familiarity with our shared discussions,
readings, and exercises.
I have been using AI extensively for many years now and can easily recognize work that has not been properly vetted or authored by a human.
Submissions that over-rely on AI (without thoughtful engagement, editing, and human input) will lose points for failing to meet expectations of depth,
accuracy, cogency, and professionalism.
AI-generated or heavily AI-assisted writing is often identifiable through the following patterns:
• Lack of contextual specificity: Writing relies on broad or abstract statements about “archaeology,” “the past,” or “human behavior”
without grounding claims in concrete data, clearly defined case studies, time periods, geographic locations, or material evidence.
• Generic or formulaic phrasing: Language sounds polished but interchangeable, using predictable academic constructions that could apply
to many topics without demonstrating focused engagement with the particular materials, readings, or examples addressed in the course.
• Absence of analytical positioning: The response summarizes concepts without showing how the writer is thinking through the evidence;
there is little indication of uncertainty, interpretation, tradeoffs, or decision-making that characterize real archaeological analysis.
• Detachment from empirical evidence: Claims are not clearly supported by specific artifacts, features, datasets, figures, or assigned
sources, or they include inaccuracies that suggest the material was synthesized rather than examined closely.
To this end, AI tools may be used only for limited support tasks (such as brainstorming, outlining, or proofreading for clarity). They may not be used
to generate substantive content, including descriptions, observations, interpretations, arguments, or comparisons. Archaeological writing requires
engagement with specific data, case studies, and contexts that must come from your own analysis or points will be deducted, whether the
disengagement comes from a lack of participation or overuse of AI…both read the same.
Effective archaeological writing should read as situated, data-driven, and interpretive, demonstrating that arguments emerge from direct
engagement with archaeological evidence and course materials, not from generalized summaries or automated synthesis.
